notes.meaning: After refusing to enter the promised land years earlier, Israel obeyed God and traveled south toward the Red Sea. They spent many long years moving around the rugged hill country of Mount Seir until God gave the word to move on. God guided their path even during this time of wandering.

The Lord finally told Moses that the people had circled the mountains long enough. Their long time of wandering was over, and they were commanded to head north toward the promised land. When God's appointed time arrives, He calls His people to move forward in faith.

God warned the people that they were about to pass along the borders of Edom, where their distant relatives descended from Esau lived. The Edomites would be terrified at the sight of such a huge crowd moving near them. Because of that fear, the Israelites were ordered to be very careful and avoid causing trouble.

The Israelites were strictly forbidden to fight the Edomites or take even a single foot of their land. The Lord Himself had assigned the mountain country of Seir to Esau's family as their home. God shows that He decides the borders of nations, and His people must respect what belongs to others.

Even though Israel was a mighty nation, they had to pay silver for all the food and drinking water they needed from Edom. They were not allowed to steal or use force just because water and food were scarce in the desert. God's people were expected to act honestly and honorably toward their neighbors.

Moses reminded the people that the Lord had blessed their hard work and watched over every step they took in the vast desert. During all forty years, God remained with them and provided everything they needed so they lacked nothing. Remembering how faithfully God provides helps us trust Him for the future.

Israel obeyed God's command and went around the borders of Edom rather than cutting through their territory. They left the desert road that ran north from the ports of Elath and Ezion-geber and headed toward the wilderness near Moab. They showed respect for their kin by choosing a longer and harder route.

When they reached Moab's borders, God told Moses not to fight or take any Moabitish territory. The Lord had granted the land of Ar to the children of Lot, Abraham's nephew, as their inheritance. God honors ancient family ties and keeps His promises to every family He has blessed.

Moses explains that a powerful and giant people known as the Emites once lived in Moab. Like the tall Anakites, they were part of the Rephaim, an ancient and fearsome race. Yet even these mighty giants could not prevent the Moabites from taking the land God had set aside for them.

Long ago, cave-dwelling people called Horites lived in Mount Seir until Esau's descendants drove them out and settled there. In the same way, Israel was now taking possession of the lands God had given them east of the Jordan River. These stories showed Israel that God can clear out any strong foe before His people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the mention of Israel taking its possession as a comment added by a later editor after the conquest of Canaan, while others see it as Moses describing the land already conquered east of the Jordan.

notes.meaning: God ordered the people to get up and cross the Brook of Zered, and they promptly obeyed. This river valley formed the natural boundary between the territory of Edom and the land of Moab. Crossing it marked the real beginning of their journey into the lands they would inherit.

It took thirty-eight years to travel from Kadesh-barnea to the crossing of the Brook of Zered. During those years, every fighting man from the older generation died in the wilderness just as the Lord had sworn. God's hand worked against that rebellious generation until the camp was completely cleared of those who refused to believe Him.

After the last soldier of the old generation had passed away, the Lord spoke to Moses once again. The long years of quiet judgment were finished, and God was now ready to lead the new generation forward. When God closes one chapter of discipline, He faithfully opens the way to His promises.

The Lord directed Moses that Israel was to march past Ar, the chief district of Moab, that very day. They were allowed to travel along Moab's borders as long as they stayed on the boundary line. God gave them clear and precise directions for every step of their journey.

As the Israelites came near the Ammonites, God ordered them not to attack or harass them in any way. Like Moab, the Ammonites were descendants of Lot, and God had given them their territory as a permanent possession. Israel had to learn that their military power was only to be used where God explicitly directed.

The land of Ammon was also once home to the Rephaim, whom the Ammonites called Zamzummites. They were a tall, numerous, and terrifying people, yet the Lord destroyed them so the Ammonites could settle there. Hearing how God cleared away giants for a neighboring nation gave Israel courage to face their own enemies.

In the same way, the Lord wiped out the Horites so Esau's family could live in Seir, and Caphtorites from Crete destroyed the Avvim near Gaza. History showed that entire nations rise and fall according to God's purpose. Israel could step out boldly, knowing that the Lord who moved ancient peoples was guiding their steps too.

God commanded Israel to cross the Arnon Valley and enter into battle against Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon. The Lord promised that He was handing Sihon over to them and would spread deep dread of Israel among the surrounding nations. When God tells His people to fight, He guarantees the victory before the battle even begins.

Moses sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth offering peaceful terms to King Sihon. They asked for simple permission to walk along the main highway without straying into fields or vineyards. This offer proved that Israel was not seeking an unnecessary fight and left Sihon without excuse if he chose war.

Moses promised to pay full price in silver for all food and water, asking only to march through on foot until reaching the Jordan River. He pointed out that the Edomites and Moabites had sold them provisions along their borders in the same way. Israel sought honest trade and peaceful passage rather than violence.

King Sihon refused to grant safe passage because the Lord made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate. His prideful decision brought about his own downfall and delivered his kingdom into Israel's hands. When rulers stubbornly reject fair and peaceful offers, they bring judgment upon themselves.

differ.view: God actively hardened Sihon's spirit as a sovereign judgment for his wickedness and as the means to fulfill his decree to destroy him.
God did not force Sihon to do evil, but permitted him to harden his own heart by removing divine restraint.

notes.meaning: The Lord announced to Moses that Sihon's defeat had already begun and urged Israel to take the land. Even before the armies clashed, God treated the victory as a sure thing. God's promises give His people the courage to step onto the battlefield without fear.

King Sihon marched out with his entire army to meet Israel in battle at Jahaz. The Lord gave Israel the victory, and they defeated Sihon, his sons, and all his forces. Victory came not through Israel's military might, but because the Lord fought for them.

Israel captured every Amorite city and completely wiped out the population under God's command of judgment. The Amorites had reached the limit of their wicked practices, so God ordered their complete destruction to protect Israel from idolatry. The Israelites kept only the farm animals and goods from the cities as spoils of war.

Israel conquered the whole territory from Aroer on the Arnon gorge all the way north to Gilead. Even though the towns were heavily fortified with tall walls that once frightened Israel, none could stand against them. When God is on our side, the highest obstacles become easy to overcome.

Even in the middle of victory, Israel carefully avoided the territory of the Ammonites, the banks of the Jabbok River, and the mountain cities God had placed off-limits. They did not let the thrill of conquest tempt them to take what was forbidden. True faithfulness means obeying God's limits just as carefully as His commands to advance.
